findings.lesson_text: Hobson's Choice was first performed at the Gaiety Theatre, Manchester, in 1916 — a venue dedicated to new, socially engaged writing.
findings.issue: The world premiere was not at the Gaiety Theatre, Manchester. The play received its world premiere on 2 November 1915 at the Princess Theatre, New York. The first English production opened on 24 June 1916 at the Apollo Theatre, London (not the Gaiety Theatre, Manchester), where it ran for 246 performances. Brighouse was indeed associated with the Gaiety Theatre in Manchester (where his earlier plays were produced), but Hobson's Choice did not premiere there.
findings.canonical_truth: World premiere: 2 November 1915, Princess Theatre, New York. English premiere: 24 June 1916, Apollo Theatre, London (ran 246 performances). The Gaiety Theatre Manchester was the home of the Manchester School generally, not the venue for this play's premiere.

findings.lesson_text: The play is set in Salford, Lancashire, in the 1880s
findings.issue: The opening stage direction of the play gives the period as simply '1880', not 'the 1880s'. The lesson text and key fact box refer to 'the 1880s' throughout all seven lessons. This is technically imprecise — Brighouse sets all four acts in 1880, not across a decade. The Wikipedia article also states 'set in Salford in 1880'. While describing the broader social context as '1880s' is acceptable shorthand for background discussion, the lesson presents it as the factual setting in ways students may repeat as precision detail in exams.
findings.canonical_truth: Opening stage direction: 'The SCENE is Salford, Lancashire, and the period is 1880.' The action of all four acts takes place within roughly one year, all in 1880. '1880s' is loose but broadly acceptable for contextual discussion; stating '1880' is more precise and preferable for exam answers about setting.

findings.lesson_text: Albert Prosser and the solicitor Fred Beenstock represent the professional middle class
findings.issue: Fred Beenstock is not a solicitor. Fred (Freddy) Beenstock is the son of Jonathan Beenstock, a corn merchant. It is Albert Prosser who is the solicitor (a junior solicitor with Prosser, Pilkington and Prosser, and Alice's suitor). The lesson conflates the two characters, describing Beenstock as a solicitor when he is from a merchant family.
findings.canonical_truth: Albert Prosser is the solicitor (age 26, son of an established solicitor, engaged to Alice). Fred Beenstock is the son of Jonathan Beenstock, a corn merchant whose cellar Hobson falls into. Beenstock is engaged to Vickey.

findings.lesson_text: "I'm not a fool, Father" is Maggie's challenge to a patriarch who assumes women exist only to serve men.
findings.issue: The exact phrase 'I'm not a fool, Father' does not appear in the primary text. The Gutenberg full text does not contain this exact wording as a Maggie line addressed to Hobson. This appears to be a paraphrase or confabulated quote that has become embedded in GCSE study materials. The line does not appear on any authoritative quotation resource for the play.
findings.canonical_truth: No confirmed line matching 'I'm not a fool, Father' verbatim exists in the primary text. It may be a loose paraphrase of Maggie's general defiance of Hobson, but should not be presented as a direct verbatim quotation or attributed as a key quote for exam use. Students who quote this in exams risk citing a line that examiners cannot verify.

findings.lesson_text: Brighouse wrote Hobson's Choice in 1916, during the suffragette era, but set it in the 1880s.
findings.issue: The play was written/completed before 1916 — it received its world premiere in November 1915, which means it was written before 1915. Brighouse did not write it 'in 1916'. 1916 is the year of the English premiere. The play was written (composed/completed) ca. 1913-1915. Key fact box and flashcard both state '1916' as the year it was 'written', which conflates composition with English premiere.
findings.canonical_truth: The play was written by Brighouse in the early 1910s and premiered in New York in November 1915. Its first English production was in 1916. Saying it was 'written in 1916' is inaccurate. More precisely: written ca. 1913-15, world premiere 2 Nov 1915, English premiere 24 June 1916.

findings.lesson_text: phrases like "By gum!" and "I've got my work cut out" are markers of Northern identity
findings.issue: 'I've got my work cut out' is presented as a Lancashire dialect marker from the play. However, this is a common English idiom — it is not specifically a Lancashire dialect phrase unique to the play. It occurs in general usage, not as a dialect marker. The lesson frames it as if it is a distinctive regional expression from the text alongside 'By gum!', which is misleading.
findings.canonical_truth: 'By gum!' is a genuine Lancashire dialect marker and appears in the play (Brighouse uses it for Willie especially). 'I've got my work cut out' is a common British English idiom, not a regional dialect marker, and should not be cited as an example of Lancashire dialect in exam answers.

findings.lesson_text: "I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll take Willie Mossop" is one of the most important lines in the play — it announces Maggie's absolute agency.
findings.issue: This exact line does not appear in the primary text. The primary text (Gutenberg and Archive.org) shows Maggie's actual words as: 'Will Mossop, you're my man. Six months I've counted on you and it's got to come out some time.' The phrase 'I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll take Willie Mossop' is a confabulated line. Additionally, the flashcard question attributes this exact line as a direct quotation from Maggie.
findings.canonical_truth: Maggie's actual words announcing her intention: 'Will Mossop, you're my man.' This is the canonical proposal line. 'I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll take Willie Mossop' is not in the primary text and should not be presented as a direct quotation or cited as a key exam quote.

findings.lesson_text: Mrs Hepworth, a wealthy customer, comes in and demands to know who made her boots ... Mrs Hepworth gives Willie her calling card ... "You're a natural born genius at making boots."
findings.issue: The line 'You're a natural born genius at making boots' is attributed to Mrs Hepworth. However, in the primary text, Mrs Hepworth says 'I've tried every shop in Manchester, and these are the best-made pair of boots I've ever had.' The 'natural born genius' line is said by Maggie to Willie, not by Mrs Hepworth. The misattribution recurs in the knowledge check ('Mrs Hepworth tells Willie: "You're a natural born genius at making boots"') and in multiple flashcards.
findings.canonical_truth: Mrs Hepworth's actual praise: 'I've tried every shop in Manchester, and these are the best-made pair of boots I've ever had.' It is Maggie who calls Willie 'a natural born genius at making boots'. The misattribution appears in the narrative text, key fact box, knowledge check, and multiple flashcards.

findings.lesson_text: Hobson's line "I'm a natural shopkeeper" is laughable
findings.issue: The line 'I'm a natural shopkeeper' is not in the primary text. No version of this line appears in the Gutenberg or Archive.org full texts. This appears to be a confabulated quotation. The lesson presents it in quotation marks and the flashcard uses it as a key quote. Students citing this in exams would be quoting a line that does not exist.
findings.canonical_truth: Hobson does not say 'I'm a natural shopkeeper' in the play. No such line appears in the primary text. The characterisation of Hobson's pompous self-belief is accurate, but this specific phrasing is not a genuine quotation and should be removed from quotation marks throughout the lesson and flashcards.

findings.lesson_text: "I'm a business woman" she declares, making it clear that this marriage is built on partnership and mutual advantage.
findings.issue: The exact phrase 'I'm a business woman' does not appear in the primary text. Multiple searches of both the Gutenberg and Archive.org full texts find no instance of this phrase. Maggie's closest sentiment is 'My brain and your hands 'ull make a working partnership' (Act 3). The lesson uses this as a key quote in the narrative, key fact box, knowledge checks, and flashcards across multiple lessons (L2, L5, L7).
findings.canonical_truth: Maggie does not say 'I'm a business woman' in the primary text. Her closest line is 'My brain and your hands 'ull make a working partnership.' The 'business woman' phrase is a well-established paraphrase used in secondary study materials but is not a verbatim quotation from the play and should not be presented in quotation marks as direct speech.

findings.lesson_text: He protests that he is already "tokened" (engaged) to Ada Figgins
findings.issue: The word 'tokened' is correctly used here. However, the lesson describes Willie as 'barely literate' — which is consistent with the play. But the accompanying description of Ada Figgins' mother arriving to 'defend Ada's claim on Willie' is a dramatisation that slightly overstates the scene. In the primary text, Ada Figgins arrives with her mother, but the scene focuses on Maggie calmly overriding them. This is not an error but a slight over-elaboration. No correction needed.
findings.canonical_truth: 'Tokened' is the correct play-text word for Willie's engagement to Ada Figgins. The Ada Figgins scene is broadly correctly described.

findings.lesson_text: Maggie and Willie's wedding celebration is a comic masterpiece ... Alice and Vickey attend reluctantly
findings.issue: The lesson assigns the wedding celebration to Act 2. In the primary text, Maggie and Willie marry in Act 2 (at St Philip's Church) but the wedding reception/celebration scene (at 39a Oldfield Road) takes place in Act 3. The lesson conflates the marriage event (Act 2) with the reception (Act 3). This mislocation of the wedding reception scene could cause students to cite the wrong act.
findings.canonical_truth: Act 2: Maggie arranges the marriage ('put the banns up') and returns to deal with her sisters and the legal framework. The wedding itself (St Philip's Church) and the reception at the new shop are in Act 3. The sisters attend the celebration in Act 3, not Act 2.

findings.lesson_text: "You told me to be strong and use the power that's come to me" he says later, acknowledging Maggie's role in his development.
findings.issue: The phrase 'You told me to be strong and use the power that's come to me' is presented as a direct quote from Willie and appears in the narrative, key fact box, and as a flashcard. This exact phrasing does not appear in authoritative sources for the play text. It appears to be a plausible paraphrase of Willie's growing confidence but is likely confabulated. If students quote this in exams it cannot be verified against the primary text.
findings.canonical_truth: Willie's actual key line when committing to Maggie in Act 1 is: 'I'll take her quick, aye, and stick to her like glue.' His acknowledgement of Maggie's influence uses different phrasing not matching 'You told me to be strong and use the power that's come to me'. This should either be verified against the full Act 4 text or removed from quotation marks.

findings.lesson_text: He falls through the cellar trapdoor of Beenstock's corn warehouse while drunk and finds himself facing a legal action for trespass and damage.
findings.issue: The lesson describes the cellar as belonging to 'Beenstock's corn warehouse' in one place and 'Beenstock's cellar trapdoor' in another, which is accurate. However, the legal action is described only as 'trespass and damage'. The actual writ in the play claims damages for 'trespass, damage to corn sacks and spying on trade secrets' — the 'spying on trade secrets' element is omitted from the lesson. This is a minor omission rather than a factual error.
findings.canonical_truth: The writ claims damages from Hobson for trespass, damage to corn sacks, and spying on trade secrets. The cellar belongs to Jonathan Beenstock & Co., Corn Merchants, of Chapel Street, Salford.

findings.lesson_text: "Hobson, you're a disgrace" is the community's verdict on a man who has squandered his business and his health.
findings.issue: The phrase 'Hobson, you're a disgrace' is presented in quotation marks with attribution to 'the community'. This exact line does not appear in the primary text. No character says this line to Hobson in the play. It appears to be a confabulated line used to summarise his social decline. The flashcard in Lesson 5 also presents 'Hobson, you're a disgrace' as a key characterisation quote.
findings.canonical_truth: No character says 'Hobson, you're a disgrace' in the play. The play does show Hobson's social fall but not through this specific line. This confabulated quote appears in the lesson text and in Lesson 5's flashcard ('Hobson, you're a disgrace — marking his fall from respected tradesman to helpless dependent') and should be removed from quotation marks.

findings.lesson_text: "I'll come into the shop, but we'll have the name Mossop & Hobson." This is the same man who could barely speak in Act 1.
findings.issue: The exact line 'I'll come into the shop, but we'll have the name Mossop & Hobson' is presented as a direct quote from Willie. The primary text shows Willie's business card reads 'William Mossop, Practical Boot and Shoe Maker, 39a, Oldfield Road, Salford' — his own independent trading name. The act 4 negotiation over the combined shop name and Willie's exact insistence on the name order has not been confirmed in the primary text extracts available, and the quoted line is not found verbatim. The knowledge check also presents 'Mossop & Hobson' as the shop's new name, derived from this quote.
findings.canonical_truth: Willie's card in Act 3 reads 'William Mossop, Practical Boot and Shoe Maker, 39a, Oldfield Road, Salford.' The Act 4 resolution does involve Maggie's conditions for returning (Willie taking over the business), and the play does end with Willie as master. However, the exact quoted line ('I'll come into the shop, but we'll have the name Mossop & Hobson') and the specific 'Mossop & Hobson' shop sign are not confirmed in the primary text and may be confabulated. The final business is widely described as Willie taking over Hobson's shop, but the precise naming convention cited has not been verified verbatim.

findings.lesson_text: A doctor diagnoses Hobson with chronic alcoholism and warns that he must stop drinking or die.
findings.issue: This is broadly correct. Dr MacFarlane does diagnose Hobson with 'chronic alcoholism' in Act 4. The lesson also describes an 'attack of delirium tremens' in the lesson narrative (L4 content_html, n5: 'After an attack of delirium tremens') but this specific phrasing is not in the main lesson text seen — it is consistent with published summaries. The lesson text as read does not say 'delirium tremens' explicitly in the excerpt, but describes 'chronic alcoholism'. This is correct.
findings.canonical_truth: Dr MacFarlane diagnoses Hobson with 'chronic alcoholism' in Act 4. Multiple secondary sources confirm this. The play also describes him suffering an 'attack of delirium tremens' per the Wikipedia summary. Both descriptions are substantively accurate.

findings.lesson_text: Maggie's key quotations: "I'm a business woman," "I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll take Willie Mossop," and "I'm not a fool, Father."
findings.issue: The key fact box lists three 'key quotations' from Maggie and presents them as the most important exam quotes. All three are unverified or confabulated: (1) 'I'm a business woman' — not found verbatim in primary text; (2) 'I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll take Willie Mossop' — not found verbatim, Maggie actually says 'Will Mossop, you're my man'; (3) 'I'm not a fool, Father' — not found verbatim in primary text. A student who memorises these three 'key quotes' would be quoting lines that likely do not appear in the play.
findings.canonical_truth: Confirmed verbatim Maggie lines from primary text: 'Will Mossop, you're my man. Six months I've counted on you and it's got to come out some time.' (proposal) and 'My brain and your hands 'ull make a working partnership.' (Act 3). The three 'key quotations' in the key fact box are all unverified and should be replaced with confirmed primary text lines.

findings.lesson_text: Mrs Hepworth recognised his talent from the start: "You're a natural born genius at making boots."
findings.issue: This repeats the misattribution from Lesson 2. 'You're a natural born genius at making boots' is attributed to Mrs Hepworth, but in the primary text this is Maggie's line. Mrs Hepworth's actual words are 'I've tried every shop in Manchester, and these are the best-made pair of boots I've ever had.' The misattribution recurs in this character analysis lesson.
findings.canonical_truth: Mrs Hepworth praises the boots ('best-made pair of boots I've ever had'), not Willie as a genius. Maggie says Willie is 'a natural born genius at making boots'. The speaker attribution is wrong in the lesson text.

findings.lesson_text: "Hobson, you're a disgrace" sums up his trajectory from respected tradesman to helpless dependent.
findings.issue: As noted in Lesson 4, this line does not appear in the primary text. The flashcard question and answer also treat this as a real key quote: 'Which line captures Hobson's eventual moral collapse? A: Hobson, you're a disgrace — marking his fall from respected tradesman to helpless dependent.' Students memorising this as an exam quote would cite a non-existent line.
findings.canonical_truth: No character says 'Hobson, you're a disgrace' in the play. This confabulated line appears in both lesson 4 and lesson 5 text, and in a lesson 5 flashcard. All instances should be removed from quotation marks.

findings.lesson_text: Flashcard: 'Which Willie line praises his own boot-making skill? A: "You're a natural born genius at making boots."'
findings.issue: The flashcard frames 'You're a natural born genius at making boots' as 'Willie's line' praising his own skill — this is doubly wrong. First, Maggie says it (not Willie, and not Mrs Hepworth). Second, it would be self-praise if Willie said it, which would be out of character. The flashcard is wrong about the speaker and the context.
findings.canonical_truth: Maggie says 'You're a natural born genius at making boots' to Willie — she is praising him. Willie does not say this about himself. The flashcard should be removed or rewritten to attribute the line to Maggie.

findings.lesson_text: When Hobson boasts "I'm a natural shopkeeper," the audience knows this is absurd
findings.issue: As flagged in Lesson 2, 'I'm a natural shopkeeper' is not in the primary text. The line recurs here in Lesson 6 in quotation marks, in both the narrative and the knowledge check match activity ('Hobson claiming to be a "natural shopkeeper" while his shop fails'). Students would not be able to find this line in the primary text.
findings.canonical_truth: Hobson does not say 'I'm a natural shopkeeper' in the play. This is a confabulated line used across multiple lessons. Remove from quotation marks or replace with a confirmed Hobson line.

findings.lesson_text: Flashcard: 'Which boastful line captures Hobson's self-delusion about his business? A: "I'm a natural shopkeeper."'
findings.issue: Same as above — the flashcard enshrines 'I'm a natural shopkeeper' as a key exam quote even though it does not appear in the primary text.
findings.canonical_truth: Remove this flashcard or replace with a confirmed Hobson line. Hobson's self-delusion is expressed through his general pomposity and actions rather than this specific verbatim line.

findings.lesson_text: "I'm not a fool, Father." Starting with this quotation, explore how Brighouse presents the theme of gender and independence
findings.issue: The practice question and key fact box use 'I'm not a fool, Father' as the exam extract question quote — the central hook for an essay question. If this line does not appear verbatim in the play, students would be writing exam essays around a quote that examiners cannot locate in the text. This is the most consequential instance of this unverified line.
findings.canonical_truth: The line 'I'm not a fool, Father' has not been confirmed in the primary text. Using it as the opening quotation for a mock exam question embeds it as an authoritative exam quote. If this line exists, it should be verified against a published edition. If it does not, the practice question and all references should be rewritten with a confirmed Maggie line.

findings.lesson_text: Practice question: '"You told me to be strong and use the power that's come to me." Starting with this quotation, explore how Brighouse presents the theme of education and self-improvement'
findings.issue: The practice question uses 'You told me to be strong and use the power that's come to me' as the exam extract. This line has not been confirmed in the primary text and appears in several places across these lessons as a key Willie quote. If unverified, using it as a practice exam extract quote is seriously misleading.
findings.canonical_truth: Willie's confirmed primary text lines include: 'I'll take her quick, aye, and stick to her like glue' (Act 1) and 'I've got my name wrote up on the windows' (Act 3). The 'You told me to be strong' line needs primary text verification before being used as an exam practice quotation.

critical_issues: Three 'key quotations' in L5 key fact box are all unverified/fabricated — Maggie's proposal ('I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll take Willie Mossop'), 'I'm a business woman', and 'I'm not a fool, Father'.

Mrs Hepworth's praise ('You're a natural born genius at making boots') is misattributed — it is Maggie's line, not Mrs Hepworth's. Appears in L2 narrative, L2 KC, L2 flashcard, L5 narrative, L5 flashcard.
'Hobson, you're a disgrace' is not in the play — appears as a quoted line in L4 and L5, and as a flashcard answer in L5.
'I'm a natural shopkeeper' is not in the play — appears as a quoted line in L2 and L6, and as a flashcard in L6.
Lesson 1 states the premiere was at the Gaiety Theatre, Manchester — it was actually the Princess Theatre, New York (1915) / Apollo Theatre, London (1916).
Lesson 1 describes Fred Beenstock as 'the solicitor Fred Beenstock' — Beenstock is a corn merchant's son; Albert Prosser is the solicitor.
'I'm a business woman' is not confirmed in primary text — used as a key quote across L2, L5, and L7.
The wedding reception is assigned to Act 2 when it belongs to Act 3.
verified_correct: Setting: Salford, Lancashire ('1880s' is a loose but acceptable summary of the precise 1880 dating).
Hobson's full name: Henry Horatio Hobson.
Willie described as working in the cellar of Hobson's shop.
Maggie is 30 years old at the start of the play.
Alice (23) courts Albert Prosser; Vickey (21) courts Fred Beenstock.
Mrs Hepworth is an upper-class customer who gives Willie her calling card.
Maggie and Willie borrow £100 from Mrs Hepworth to set up their shop.
New shop at 39a Oldfield Road, Salford.
Hobson falls through the trapdoor into Jonathan Beenstock & Co. corn warehouse.
Trespass damages original claim £1,000, settled at £500, split as dowries for Alice and Vickey.
Dr MacFarlane diagnoses Hobson with chronic alcoholism in Act 4.
Willie's word 'tokened' for his engagement to Ada Figgins.
'By gum!' is correctly identified as Willie's dialect exclamation.
Manchester School of dramatists: Brighouse alongside Stanley Houghton and Allan Monkhouse.
The pub Hobson frequents is the Moonraker's Inn (lesson says 'Moonraker's' — correct).
The play's subtitle is 'A Lancashire Comedy in Four Acts'.
Maggie's actual proposal line: 'Will Mossop, you're my man' — correctly quoted in L1 flashcard context but then overshadowed by the fabricated 'I'll tell you what I'll do' line.
Willie's line when committing to Maggie: 'I'll take her quick, aye, and stick to her like glue' — not mentioned in the lessons but consistent with primary text.
